Over the past three decades the logistics of field research have changed a great deal, and most of the change has come from ordinary planning rather than from any single breakthrough. A typical expedition begins months in advance with a long series of meetings about budgets, shipping schedules, equipment lists and medical clearance. The people who run those meetings are rarely the same people who travel, which produces a steady traffic of messages between offices in different time zones. Each item has a serial number, a maintenance history and a designated owner, and every box is weighed twice because aircraft space is expensive and unforgiving.

Weather is the other constant theme. Forecasts are checked several times a day, and decisions about whether to fly are made early in the morning when the wind is usually calmest. A delay of one day can ripple through the schedule, pushing a later flight into a window already reserved for somebody else. Experienced managers therefore build slack into every plan, even though the people paying for the work often ask why nothing is scheduled more tightly. Food and fuel are ordered together because both arrive on the same aircraft and both must be stored in the same cold space. There is a running argument about whether canned goods or dried goods travel better, and the answer seems to depend on the year, the route and the mood of the person packing.

Teams are assembled from many institutions, and a single project may involve a dozen departments with different rules about insurance, reporting and the ownership of samples. The paperwork is tedious, but it prevents disputes later, when a sample turns out to matter and everyone remembers having helped collect it. Crates arrive at the staging building, are signed for twice, and are stacked in a corridor where nobody can walk past without tripping. By the time the aircraft finally leaves, the preparation has consumed more effort than the fieldwork itself.

The instruments themselves are surprisingly modest: a drill, a set of probes, a laptop with software written by a student who has since graduated, and a great many batteries. Spare parts are packed for every joint and every cable, because a replacement cannot be ordered from the field no matter how much it costs. Everything that comes back is cleaned, counted and logged before it disappears into a warehouse for the winter.

Most participants say they would do it again, and most of them mean it. The ice does not care about any of this. It remains where it always was, patient and indifferent, while the people who study it come and go with their boxes, budgets and carefully written plans. Last season the team from the university finally reached Antarctica after two extra days in a staging town, and the samples they carried back are still being analysed in a laboratory.
